title: A third of the can, two thirds of the can

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A cylinder is a circle stacked through a height: base area pi *r* squared, times height *h*.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A cone narrows from a circular base to a point. Match its base radius and straight height to the can.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Turn the cone into a measuring cup. Careful measuring shows this.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Pour one full cone. The water rises to one third.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Refill. Pour again. Watch the level rise to two thirds.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Refill. The third pour rises all the way to the brim. Exactly one can.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: One cone holds one third of pi *r* squared *h*. Remember the third: the whole can is too much.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Find the cone's volume with radius nine inches and height seventeen inches.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Its can holds eighty-one pi times seventeen: thirteen hundred seventy-seven pi cubic inches.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Divide by three: four hundred fifty-nine pi cubic inches. If asked for *a* in *a* pi, give four hundred fifty-nine.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A sphere is a ball. Its can fits exactly: same radius, and two radii tall.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Fill the space around the ball with water. Transfer just that water into an identical empty can.

do.text: Measure the space around the ball

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Watch the water rise. It fills one third of the can. So the ball occupies the other two thirds.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: These are measured relationships. Their mathematical proofs come in a later course.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The can holds pi *r* squared times two *r*: two pi *r* cubed.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Take two thirds. Two thirds times two gives four thirds.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Cube the radius: it appears twice in the base area, once more in the height.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Given a diameter of six centimeters, halve it. The radius is three centimeters.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: For radius three centimeters, the can is six centimeters tall and holds fifty-four pi cubic centimeters.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The ball holds two thirds of that: thirty-six pi cubic centimeters.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A hemisphere is half a sphere. Cut through the center: each half holds eighteen pi cubic centimeters.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Keep pi for an exact answer. Use three point one four only when the question asks.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A cone is a third of its can; a ball is two thirds of its can.
